topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: AI already touches what you see
topics.description: AI already shapes the images you see every day. Your feed, your filters, image search, auto-enhance: a machine sorted or changed them before you ever opened a tool on purpose.
evidence: Point to three places in a normal day where an algorithm picked or changed an image they saw
Explain why an image from a search is already a sorted result, not a neutral one
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to trace one image on their moodboard back to how it reached them, and to name the machines that touched it on the way.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Prediction, not understanding
topics.description: A generative model predicts what is likely to come next from patterns in its data. It does not know truth, want anything, or understand a site, and everything else you learn rests on that gap.
evidence: Explain in their own words why a model can give a confident answer that is wrong
Use a design example to show the difference between 'the model predicts' and 'the model knows'
topics.critPrompt: When an AI output is wrong in crit, can the student explain it as a bad prediction rather than a 'glitch'?

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Where the model's world comes from
topics.description: A model's whole world is its training data, and raw data is only the bottom rung of a ladder that climbs to information, then knowledge, then judgment. What the model was never shown does not exist for it, and what it saw too often takes over.
evidence: Explain why a model draws some building types well and others badly
Name one thing from their own world that the training data probably left out
topics.critPrompt: Ask what the model's version of 'an Indian street' gets wrong, and why the data would make it so.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Every output is a draw
topics.description: The same prompt can give you a different result each time, because each output is one pick from a range of possibilities — a draw, not an answer. Turn the randomness setting down and the picks repeat more often, but they are still picks. That is what makes this medium rich, and also what makes it a casino.
evidence: Run the same prompt three times and explain why the results can differ
Explain what 'sampled' means, using dice or a shuffled deck as the example
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say why re-rolling the same prompt is not iteration?

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Pattern is not precedent
topics.description: A pattern of 'what courtyards tend to look like' is not a precedent. A precedent is a real, studied building with a site, a climate, a structure, and an author — the model has patterns, the discipline has precedents.
evidence: Compare an AI-made courtyard with a real, documented precedent, and name what the real one has that the pattern is missing
Explain why calling a generated image a 'reference' is a mistake about what kind of thing it is
topics.critPrompt: In a precedent-study crit, can the student tell what they learned from a building apart from what they just liked in an image?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: How words and images become numbers
topics.description: Words get split into tokens. Images become grids of numbers. The model never sees your drawing, only the numbers behind it. Once you get that, most of the mystery goes away.
evidence: Show, in rough terms, how a sentence gets broken into tokens
Explain why 'the model sees my image' really means 'the model does math on numbers pulled from my image'
topics.critPrompt: Can the student tell a classmate, in plain words, what the model actually gets when they upload a sketch?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Latent space, the field of possibilities
topics.description: The model holds a squeezed-down space where points that sit close together look alike. Making an image is really moving around in it. A prompt drops a pin in the field of possibilities, and every re-roll lands nearby. Directing design is learning to steer in this space.
evidence: Explain why two prompts that are close in wording give you similar-looking images
Use a map-and-terrain picture to describe what a prompt does inside latent space
topics.critPrompt: When every result has the same look, can the student name the corner of latent space they are stuck in, and say what small change to the prompt would move them out?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Images out of noise
topics.description: Diffusion models start with pure noise and clean it up one step at a time, with the prompt steering each step. The picture is not pulled from a library. It slowly forms out of the noise. That is why a generated image can look right everywhere and still be made up.
evidence: Talk through the denoising steps in plain words, using a row of images from noise to finished picture
Explain why every detail can look believable while none of it is actually correct
topics.critPrompt: Can the student explain why the model drew a staircase that leads nowhere, without calling it a bug?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Language models, the next-word engine
topics.description: A large language model does one thing: it predicts the next token. It does this at such a huge scale that the guessing starts to look like real thinking. Knowing what is really going on keeps you in charge of what to trust and what to check.
evidence: Explain how guessing the next word, over and over, can build a paragraph that reads like a real argument
Give one job where next-word guessing is good enough, and one where you must check the answer
topics.critPrompt: When a student quotes what an LLM says about a building code, do they flag it as a guess that still needs checking?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Dreaming engines
topics.description: These are the models that make things up freely. They are best at mood, at what-ifs, and at images you could never have drawn yourself. Their gift is that they take you somewhere new. Their danger is that somewhere new can look finished when it is not really designed.
evidence: Name the moments in a project where free invention is the right tool
Make a study with a dreaming engine, and say what question you were asking it to answer
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say why this stage of their project needed free dreaming instead of sticking to real inputs?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Grounded generators
topics.description: These models are held to real inputs: a plan, a photo, a control image, a model of the real site. Their gift is that they stay true to what already exists. The catch is simple. The input has to be good enough to be worth staying true to.
evidence: Run the same idea through a free generation and a grounded one, then compare what stayed the same
Explain what a control input locks in place and what it still leaves free
topics.critPrompt: Is the student grounding on inputs that carry real design thinking, or just dressing up a weak drawing in a strong style?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: What the machine cannot hold
topics.description: The model has no site, no gravity, no weather, no client, and no sense that choices have consequences. Its mistakes are not random — they repeat in the same ways, and the trained eye learns to check for each one. Some of those limits are structural and stay; others are only data gaps that retraining can close, so the discipline is to re-test each new version, not to assume.
evidence: List five mistakes that generated building images make again and again
Explain which failure modes are structural and which are data gaps that retraining can close, and why the eye must re-test every new version
topics.critPrompt: Shown a good-looking render, can the student name which missing limit would break it first: structure, climate, code, or cost?

grounding.ref: Chatterjee et al., 2024 — Getting it Right / SPRIGHT (arXiv:2404.01197)

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Teaching the model your language
topics.description: Fine-tuning and LoRA training let you teach a model your own visual language, using your own body of work. The point here is to know when a studio should own a trained model instead of renting a look through prompts.
evidence: Explain what a fine-tune can change in a model and what it cannot
Make the case for when your own body of work is worth training on, and when prompting is enough
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say what fifty images of their own work would teach a model, and what it would still not know about their judgment?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Naming what you see
topics.description: Threshold, datum, grain, mass, aperture, parti. These precise words are not decoration. They are the raw material of every brief you write, to a person or a machine.
evidence: Describe a photographed space in ten precise spatial terms
Replace three vague words ('nice', 'modern', 'cool') with terms that carry real spatial meaning
topics.critPrompt: In crit, does the student describe their own scheme in words a builder or a model could act on?

grounding.ref: standard architectural pedagogy (e.g. Ching, Architecture: Form, Space & Order)

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Words for material and light
topics.description: Raking light, patina, specular, matte, monsoon overcast, tungsten warmth. Material and light are where briefs go vague most often. They are also where a precise brief pays off most in a generated image.
evidence: Describe the same wall under three different lights, using different words for each
Write a material description precise enough that two readers imagine the same surface
topics.critPrompt: Can the student change the light in an image with words alone, without touching a slider?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The prompt is a brief
topics.description: A prompt is not a wish. It is a brief you hand a machine. It follows the same discipline as a brief you hand a consultant: intent, constraints, exclusions, criteria. The oldest skill in practice, aimed at the newest tool.
evidence: Rewrite a one-line wish as a structured brief and show the difference in outputs
Take a failed generation and point to the missing part of the brief that caused it
topics.critPrompt: Show the student a weak output: do they reach for the re-roll, or for the brief?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The seven-slot brief
topics.description: Subject · composition · material · light · view · mood · exclusions. This scaffold makes a visual brief complete by design. Any slot you leave empty is a decision you hand to the model.
evidence: Write a complete seven-slot brief for a given design intent
Check a peer's brief and name the empty slots the model filled on its own
topics.critPrompt: For any image the student shows, can they produce the seven-slot brief behind it, and defend each slot as a decision?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Exclusions are design decisions
topics.description: What you forbid shapes what you get. An exclusion carries as much design intent as anything you include. It is the negative space of the brief.
evidence: Add three exclusions to a brief and show how the outputs change
Name a default the model kept adding until you excluded it by name
topics.critPrompt: Can the student name what they had to forbid to make the image theirs?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Decode the messy brief
topics.description: Boil a long, messy, contradictory client brief down to its design drivers. This is the oldest act in practice. It is now also the first step of any serious AI workflow.
evidence: Reduce a two-page client email to five design drivers with priorities
Point out which stated wants conflict, then propose the fix the brief itself points to
topics.critPrompt: Given a messy brief, does the student find the project inside it, or just summarise the text?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Generate the brief, then red-pen it
topics.description: Now run it backwards. From three vague client lines, use AI to draft a full brief. Then mark it up as its editor. Generation is a first draft of thinking. Editing is where authorship lives.
evidence: Generate a full brief from minimal context and red-pen it for wrong assumptions
Name which generated assumptions were useful provocations and which were traps
topics.critPrompt: Does the student treat the generated brief as a proposal to be edited, or as an answer to be obeyed?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Curation is diagnosis
topics.description: Reading a batch is not shopping. It is diagnosis. The batch shows what your brief really asked for, which is almost never what you meant.
evidence: Sort a 12-image batch into families. For each family, say what it reveals about the brief.
Find the gap between the brief you meant and the brief the model heard, using the outputs alone.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what the batch taught them about their own brief. Not which image they like.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Fifty images is gambling
topics.description: Making fifty images and picking the closest one is gambling, not iteration. Real iteration changes one thing in the brief each cycle and knows why. The casino and the studio use the same machine. The difference is the discipline.
evidence: Run five cycles. Change one named thing in the brief each time, and say why.
Explain why making a pile and picking one lands on the model's taste, not yours.
topics.critPrompt: For the image on the wall, can the student show the chain of decisions that made it, cycle by cycle?

grounding.ref: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou & Velloso, 2024 (CHI; arXiv:2403.11164)

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Visual forensics
topics.description: Read an AI image for evidence. Look for structure that cannot stand, light that comes from nowhere, materials that lie, joints that resolve nothing. A trained eye treats every generated image as a witness to cross-examine.
evidence: Mark up a render. Point to every part of the structure and lighting that could not be real.
Take three good-looking images. Rank them by how much of each would survive an engineer.
topics.critPrompt: Hand the student a beautiful image. How long before they find the load path that isn't there?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: An image is not a proposal
topics.description: A beautiful image is not a finished proposal. One frame carries six different things: image, idea, geometry, buildability, atmosphere, and story. It can hold each of them, or fake them.
evidence: Take one image. Check it across all six: image, idea, geometry, buildability, atmosphere, story.
Show one case where the image is strong but the idea is missing. Then show the reverse.
topics.critPrompt: When the student pins up a render, ask which of the six layers it really holds. Watch whether they already know.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The red pen is authorship
topics.description: Mark up AI output like a crit: what stays, what goes, what the next cycle must fix. That is the act that turns generated material into authored work. The red pen, not the prompt, is where the designer signs.
evidence: Red-pen an output. Give clear, ranked corrections the maker can act on.
Turn that markup into the next cycle's revised brief.
topics.critPrompt: Is the student's markup a set of design decisions, or just a list of complaints?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The iteration log
topics.description: A steady record: brief version, output, judgment, next move. The log is what lets you defend an AI process in a jury, show it in a portfolio, and improve it over time.
evidence: Keep a full log across one design exercise.
Rebuild the whole decision chain for a reviewer, using the log alone.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student show their working, the way a mathematician must, from first brief to final frame?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Taste is trained
topics.description: Taste is a reference library, a set of positions, and a growing sense of what is yours and what is noise. It is not a gift. You build it on purpose, and it is the one filter the machine cannot give you.
evidence: Build a 20-item reference library. Write one line on why each item earned its place.
State one position you hold that would change how you brief a model.
topics.critPrompt: Ask what the student has cut from their references this term, and why. Taste shows in the deletions.

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Whose work taught the machine
topics.description: These tools learned from other people's photos, drawings, and buildings. Most of those people were never asked. When you use the tool, you work inside that fact. You cannot step around it.
evidence: Explain what it means when a model can copy a living photographer's style
Say where they stand on prompts that name a living designer to borrow their style
topics.critPrompt: If a student prompts 'in the style of' a living architect, could they defend it to that architect's face?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: The tilted mirror
topics.description: A model leans toward what the internet photographs most. The default house drifts American. The default city drifts north. The global south is under-photographed. So briefing with care from here is an act of representation, not just craft. This bias is built in, and it is yours to correct. And the tilt runs deeper than which streets are photographed: a model can copy a vernacular's forms while missing the climate and material reasoning that made them — resemblance, not reasoning.
evidence: Show the default drift with a bare prompt, then fix it with a precise one
Explain why their own well-documented context is training data the world is missing
topics.critPrompt: Can the student make the tool draw their street, not the internet's idea of a street? And can they say what it took?

grounding.ref: Pishahang & Badiei, 2026 — From Clay to Code (arXiv:2601.00029)

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Provenance chains
topics.description: Provenance asks four things. Where did the data come from? Where did the model come from? Where did this output come from? And who may use it, for what? Provenance is a chain of custody. Tracking it is a professional habit, like citing your sources.
evidence: Trace the provenance of one model and one output they used, as far as public facts allow
Explain a licence at a practical level: what it permits, and what it can spoil downstream
topics.critPrompt: For an image in their portfolio, can the student state its provenance chain in three sentences?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Generation is not free
topics.description: Every generation spends energy, water, and money somewhere. Being aware of that cost is not guilt. It is the same discipline that makes an architect price a detail before drawing five hundred of them. And it is part of the same climate responsibility you already carry as a designer.
evidence: Estimate the rough cost of their last generation session, in energy and money
Show how a tighter brief would have reached the same result for less
topics.critPrompt: Ask what the student's fifty rejected images cost. And ask whether a loose brief or the model paid for them.

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Who is the author
topics.description: AI-assisted is not the same as AI-authored. Authorship follows judgment. It lives in the brief, the choices you keep, the red pen, the chain of decisions. Attribution and honest disclosure follow once you can show that chain.
evidence: Make a claim they could defend about who authored one of their AI-assisted works
Write the one-line disclosure they would attach to it in a competition entry
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what in this work is theirs. The strength of the answer is the mastery.

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Honest in the room
topics.description: Show AI-assisted work honestly to clients, juries, and the public. Be clear about what is a guess and what is resolved. Be clear about what the machine made and what you drew. Trust is the only asset a practice keeps for good.
evidence: Present an AI-assisted study and name its status clearly: is it speculation or a real proposal?
Explain the risk of passing a generated image off as a finished design
topics.critPrompt: In the mock client meeting, does the student's language keep the image's status honest, even under pressure?

grounding.ref: professional codes of conduct on honest representation (COA/AIA, general provisions)

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Verify before you build on it
topics.description: Treat every AI claim as a guess until you check it against a primary source. Codes, bye-laws, and product specs are where a wrong answer becomes your liability, so verification is the habit that keeps AI a help and not a risk.
evidence: Catch one confident but wrong AI claim by checking it against a primary source
Keep their research notes split into verified and unverified
topics.critPrompt: Ask which facts in the site analysis came from AI, and which of those the student actually checked. The ratio is the grade.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Site research with a fast assistant
topics.description: Use AI to speed up site, context, climate, and programme research, with verification always attached. Let the AI draft the questions, but let primary sources give the answers.
evidence: Build a site-research dossier with AI help, and cite a source for every fact the design leans on
Point to one place where an AI-drafted question improved their research direction
topics.critPrompt: Does the dossier clearly separate what the AI suggested from what a real source confirmed?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Map the workflow before adding AI
topics.description: Draw your real workflow first, every step from brief to submission, before any AI enters it. A workflow is never neutral — each one carries assumptions about how design should happen — so mapping it shows both where AI reduces friction and the worldview the process quietly encodes.
evidence: Draw their real, current workflow for one type of project
Mark the three hardest steps, then argue which ones AI actually helps with, if any
topics.critPrompt: Ask where AI should NOT enter the workflow, and why. A clear 'no' proves the map is real.

grounding.ref: When the Lab Became a Language — when-the-lab-became-a-language-a

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: AI across the project arc
topics.description: AI fits differently at each stage of a project: research, brief, massing, iteration, drawings, communication. The rule for where it goes stays simple — reduce friction, not judgment — because the real risk is not being replaced by the machine but working with an undirected one; your job is to direct it like a brilliant, tireless junior. This is a friction map, not a tool list.
evidence: Place each possible AI use on the project arc, and defend where it sits
Name one stage where they choose to keep AI out on purpose
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say where in their project AI works for them, and where it would replace the very part that is the point?

grounding.ref: The AI Design Director Protocol — the-ai-design-director-protocol

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Render to reel, and when not to
topics.description: Image-to-video turns a still into motion cheaply. The real question is about story: does the motion serve the design, or is it just polish on a scheme you have not resolved yet?
evidence: Make a short motion study from a still, and say what design idea the motion serves
Name one case where they chose not to animate, and say why
topics.critPrompt: Ask what the video shows that the still could not. If the only answer is 'it moves', the exercise failed.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: From chatbots to studio systems
topics.description: The path runs from chatbot to custom assistant to agent to full studio system. See the direction, and you can read the next five years as one clear trend, not a parade of new products.
evidence: Explain the difference between asking a chatbot a question and handing a task to an agent
Describe one studio task that turns into a standing system instead of a one-time session
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say what changes in who is responsible when AI acts over time, instead of just answering once?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Two paths to capability
topics.description: When a studio wants more than off-the-shelf apps, it faces a choice: build custom tools, or run agentic workflows on general-purpose systems. This is a way to decide, not a list of products to buy.
evidence: Frame a real studio need as a choice between building a tool and orchestrating one, with the trade-offs named
Say which path a studio's size and skills can actually support
topics.critPrompt: Given a studio scenario, does the student reach for the decision, or just for a brand name?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Judgment is the job
topics.description: This is the capstone. AI multiplies options, speeds up iteration, and floods the field with images. That makes good judgment rarer, and so worth more. The architect’s job becomes the interface between intelligences — aligning human intuition, technical expertise, and machine reasoning into one coherent space — and still carrying the responsibility. This is not a consolation prize. It is the job.
evidence: Write down their own working contract with these tools
Show one full project where every AI contribution passed through a judgment they can state
topics.critPrompt: The final crit question: what did you decide that AI could not have decided for you, and where is the proof in the work?

grounding.ref: judgment is the job — capstone position (Beyond Automation lineage)
The Architect as Systems Thinker — the-architect-as-systems-thinker

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: What the licence lets you do
topics.description: Open-weight models and paid API services give you very different rights over what you make. Learn to read those rights early. Check whether an output can be published, sold, or used for commercial work before a deliverable depends on the answer.
evidence: For one model they use, find whether its terms allow commercial use of outputs, and point to where the terms say so
Explain the real difference between running open weights on your own machine and using a paid API, in terms of what you may keep and sell
topics.critPrompt: Before putting an AI-made image in a paid deliverable, can the student name the licence or terms that allow it? Or are they just assuming they may?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Your work is in the scrape
topics.description: Public image datasets are built by scraping the open web without asking. That means a student's own uploaded portfolio may already be training data. Consent is mostly missing here. Opt-out, where it exists at all, comes only after the fact.
evidence: Explain how a public dataset ends up holding images no one was asked to give
Describe what it would mean for their own posted work to sit in a training set, and what recourse, if any, they would have
topics.critPrompt: Does the student see that 'scraped from the web' includes the web they publish to, not just distant strangers' work?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: The render that lies
topics.description: A generated view can show a place that does not exist. It can erase a neighbour, flatten a slope, invent a heritage wall, or show an 'as-built' that was never built. Showing that image as the real site condition is a misrepresentation. It is not a style choice.
evidence: In a generated site image, spot one invented condition that could mislead a client or an authority
Draw the line between fair speculation and a false claim about what is really on the ground
topics.critPrompt: When a student shows a generated context view, do they flag what is real site and what the model invented, before anyone has to ask?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: The people inside the model
topics.description: Human labour makes these models usable. People give feedback and moderate content. Much of this work is done in the Global South for low pay. Some of it exposes workers to disturbing material. That labour sits in the supply chain of every prompt.
evidence: Explain what human annotators and moderators add between a raw model and a usable assistant
Draw the parallel between the annotator behind a prompt and the labourer behind a building material
topics.critPrompt: When the student talks about 'the model', can they name the human work that made it safe to use, like the moderation work documented in the Kenya case?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Trained once, used forever
topics.description: A model is trained once, at a large one-time cost. Then it runs billions of times. Industry analyses now point to that everyday use, called inference and spread across every prompt, as where most of the ongoing energy and water use builds up. Hold this at the level of rough scale, not exact numbers.
evidence: Tell the one-time cost of training apart from the repeating cost of everyday use, in plain words
Explain how 'my one prompt is tiny' and 'inference is the bigger footprint' can both be true at once
topics.critPrompt: Can the student reason about the environmental cost at the right rough scale, without inventing a number or pretending the cost is zero?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: The data centre is a building
topics.description: The infrastructure that runs AI is architecture. It is power-hungry, water-cooled, and more and more often briefed to designers. Our field learned to read embodied carbon in concrete and steel. We cannot look away now that the carbon moves into the server hall. This is the same climate responsibility, in a new building type.
evidence: Describe the data centre as a building type, with its own energy, water, and siting logic
Link the studio's embodied-carbon vocabulary to the infrastructure behind the tools it uses
topics.critPrompt: Does the student treat AI's physical infrastructure as architecture they could be asked to design, or as someone else's distant problem?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Declaring AI in your submission
topics.description: Using AI in coursework without declaring it can cross from help into academic dishonesty. The literate student learns the new norm: declare what the machine did, the way you cite a source. Do not hide it.
evidence: Write an honest one-line note of how AI was used in a piece of their own submitted work
Tell apart a use that only needs declaring from a use that would be dishonest even if declared
topics.critPrompt: If asked how AI touched this submission, does the student have a truthful answer ready, or does the question catch them out?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: New forms of plagiarism
topics.description: AI raises plagiarism questions the old rules never saw coming. Passing a generated image off as hand-drawn. Reusing a peer's prompt as your own. Handing in a model's composition as your own work. Naming these early keeps the student on the right side of them.
evidence: Name three specific acts with AI that would count as academic dishonesty, and say why
Explain why a generated image shown as a hand drawing is a misrepresentation, however good it looks
topics.critPrompt: Can the student tell using a tool apart from passing its output off as their own hand, and say where the line sits?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Disclosure in competitions
topics.description: Competitions, juries, and publications now ask what was AI-generated, even while the norms are still unsettled. Knowing when and how to disclose is part of entering. So is writing the disclosure line before you submit.
evidence: Draft the AI-use disclosure statement for a real or mock competition entry
Argue why disclosing early protects the author more than staying silent, even when no rule forces it
topics.critPrompt: For work headed to a jury or a publication, has the student decided what to disclose and written it down, or are they hoping the question never comes up?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Prompting a living craft
topics.description: Prompting 'in the style of' kasuti, kolam, or another regional craft takes the surface of a living tradition and gives its makers nothing back. The question is not whether the model can copy it. It is whether you should, and on whose terms.
evidence: Explain the difference between studying a craft tradition and prompting a flat imitation of it
Take a position you could defend on when 'in the style of' a shared craft is homage, and when it is extraction
topics.critPrompt: If the student prompts a living craft tradition, could they defend the act to a maker who carries that lineage, not just to a jury?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Documenting is representing
topics.description: When a community, region, or vernacular is under-photographed, documenting it well is more than craft. It decides whether the next model sees it at all. Data dignity starts with who bothers to record their own context, and how faithfully they do it.
evidence: Document one under-photographed place or practice from their own context, faithfully enough to correct a model's default
Explain why careful local documentation is an act of representation, not just archiving
topics.critPrompt: Does the student see recording their own under-photographed context as representation the world's data is missing, and take the responsibility that carries?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: The rules are still forming
topics.description: AI governance in India and worldwide is still forming, not settled. Know that frameworks and guidance exist and keep changing. Do not pretend a fixed rulebook already governs design practice. Watch the space. Do not invent what is in it.
evidence: Name one real AI governance or literacy framework, and say honestly what it settles and what it does not yet settle
Explain why saying 'an AI law requires X' without a primary source is a mistake
topics.critPrompt: Can the student hold the honest line, that the rules are forming and must be tracked, without inventing a law or waving regulation away as irrelevant?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Clear the rights before shipping
topics.description: Before an AI-assisted image goes into a deliverable, someone must clear the rights. That means the model licence, permission for any reference image, and the client agreement. Run this checklist as a studio habit, learned young. It is not a lawyer's afterthought.
evidence: Run a short IP-clearance pass on one AI-assisted output: model terms, reference permissions, client consent
Point out which reference images in a workflow they had no right to feed the model
topics.critPrompt: Before the student ships, do they run the clearance pass by reflex, model, reference, client, or find the rights problem only when challenged?

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Name, brief, audit, refuse
topics.description: When the model returns a flat, culturally generic default, the literate response is four moves, in order. Name the flattening. Brief against it. Audit the output for what is left. And refuse to ship an image that reads as anywhere-in-the-world when the project is right here.
evidence: Take a flat default output and run all four moves, ending in a re-briefed, audited result
Explain why refusing to ship the flat image is the move that carries the weight, not the styling
topics.critPrompt: Faced with a beautiful but placeless default, does the student run the four moves in order, or ship the pretty image and call it warm and modern?

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Learned, not programmed
topics.description: Older design software follows rules a person wrote by hand. These systems are the opposite: nobody wrote their rules, the machine just picked up patterns from millions of examples, and those patterns are all it has to work from.
evidence: Explain the difference between a rule a programmer wrote and a pattern the machine learned from examples
Name one design task a rule-based tool does reliably, and one that only a pattern-learner even attempts
topics.critPrompt: Ask whether a given tool's behaviour was written by a programmer or learned from data, and how they can tell.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: AI is not one thing
topics.description: 'AI' is not one tool but rings inside rings: any system that does a task, then the ones that learn from data, then the deep-learning ones, and at the centre the generative ones that make new content. The first useful question about any 'AI' claim is which ring it means.
evidence: Put four named systems in the right ring: a spam filter, a translator, an image classifier, and a chatbot
Rewrite a sweeping 'AI will…' headline into an exact claim about just one ring
topics.critPrompt: When a student says 'AI', ask which ring they mean, and whether their statement still holds once it is narrowed down.

grounding.ref: Russell & Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 2021

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: What 'model' really means
topics.description: In this field a 'model' is not an app you open or a mind that answers — it is a trained function that turns your input into a spread of likely outputs, each with its own odds. The app you click is just a wrapper built around it.
evidence: In one sentence each, tell the model apart from the app, the brand, and 'a mind'
Explain why a model returns a spread of likely outputs instead of one stored answer
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student which part of the tool is 'the model', and watch whether they point at the app icon or the trained core underneath.

grounding.ref: Wolfram, What Is ChatGPT Doing… and Why Does It Work?, 2023

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Learning time and using time
topics.description: A model has two phases: training, the long and costly past when it soaked up its patterns, and inference, the quick moment it answers each time you prompt it. It is not learning from you as you work. The learning already happened, then stopped.
evidence: In plain words, separate what happens during training from what happens during inference
Explain why a chatbot does not 'remember' yesterday's chat unless the system feeds it back on purpose
topics.critPrompt: Ask whether the model is learning from their project as they use it, and have them defend the answer using the two phases.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Naming versus making
topics.description: Some models sort things that already exist: this is a chair, this façade is Art Deco. Others make something that was not there before, and most tools a design student meets are the making kind, so knowing which kind you hold tells you what you can trust it for.
evidence: Sort a list of tasks into 'classify' and 'generate', and defend each choice
Explain why a classifier can be checked against a right answer and a generator usually cannot
topics.critPrompt: Ask whether the tool in front of them is naming what exists or making what doesn't, and how that changes the way you judge its output.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Finding versus inventing
topics.description: A search brings back things that already exist somewhere, and you can trace each one to a source. A generator invents a fresh answer that may look sourced but comes from nowhere, which is why a generated 'reference' can point to nothing real.
evidence: Explain why a search result has a source and a generated passage may have none
Show a case where an invented citation or image was taken for a real, found one
topics.critPrompt: When a student cites something the tool produced, ask whether it was found or invented, and whether they checked.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: The model's world is closed
topics.description: Everything the model can use is second-hand, limited, and frozen at the moment training stopped. It never stood on a site, and it knows nothing that was not in its data or given to it in the prompt. Its world ends where its data ends.
evidence: Name two things about a real site the model cannot know unless someone tells it
Explain what a training cutoff is, and why it makes the model wrong about recent things
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what the model could not possibly know about their site, and where that knowledge would have to come from instead.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: What a chatbot is made of
topics.description: A chatbot is not one thing but a stack of parts: a trained model, a sampler that picks each word, a hidden system prompt that sets its manners, and the running context of your chat. Name the parts and the black box becomes something you can steer.
evidence: Label the parts of a chatbot and say what each one does: model, sampler, system prompt, and context
Explain why the same model can act very differently inside two different chat apps
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student which part caused a given behaviour: the model, the sampler, or the hidden setup.

grounding.ref: Karpathy, Intro to Large Language Models, 2023

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Confident is not correct
topics.description: A model sounds smooth and sure because it picks the most likely words, so that confidence is a fact about the writing, not proof the content is true. The smoothest answer and the wrong answer can be the very same answer.
evidence: Get a model to state one claim with full confidence that they can check and prove wrong
Explain why smooth writing and correct writing are two different things, using how outputs are made
topics.critPrompt: When a student trusts an answer, ask what they are trusting: its confidence, or a source they checked.

grounding.ref: Guo et al., On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks, 2017

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: People are in the loop
topics.description: Human choices run all the way through the system: people gathered and labelled the data, people tuned the model by rating better and worse answers, and a person still decides what to do with each output. The machine is never working alone.
evidence: Name three points where human choices shaped a model before the student ever prompted it
Explain why keeping a person in charge of the final call is a design choice, not a weakness
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to find the humans in a workflow that looks fully automatic: before the model, inside it, and after it.

grounding.ref: Christiano et al., Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences, 2017

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: From CAD to generative
topics.description: Design has taken in wave after wave of new tools: hand drawing, CAD, BIM, parametric, each learned late and in a hurry. Generative AI is the newest wave, but it is different in kind — the older tools changed how the work got made, while this one is cognitive infrastructure, a medium you think with that reaches into authorship and judgment themselves, not just one more piece of software that makes pictures.
evidence: Place generative AI in the line of CAD, BIM, and parametric tools, and say what each wave changed
Argue one way AI is different in kind from the earlier tool waves, not just bigger
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what earlier tool shifts teach about this one, and where the comparison stops holding.

grounding.ref: AI differs in kind from earlier design-tool waves — it touches authorship, not only workflow
The Architect as Systems Thinker — the-architect-as-systems-thinker

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Why this matters here, now
topics.description: AI is arriving in Indian architecture education faster than the answer to who will teach it, and its built environment is under-photographed — exactly the material these tools handle worst. So building real literacy from here is not catching up, it is an act of representation.
evidence: Explain why an Indian design student cannot just borrow a Western way of framing AI literacy
Name one way the local built environment is left out of what these tools were trained on
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what their own context gives them that the model lacks, and why that is an edge rather than a drawback.

grounding.ref: literacy briefed from an under-imaged context is representation, not catch-up

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Attention, the model's glance back
topics.description: Before it picks each token, the model weighs which earlier tokens matter most for what comes next. It is like a designer glancing back over a brief. Attention is picky and limited, and what it picks is what actually steers the result.
evidence: Explain, with no math, why a detail twenty lines back can still shape the next word, or get ignored
Describe attention as weighing, not reading, using the picture of someone skimming a brief
topics.critPrompt: When a model keeps one rule and drops another, can the student explain it as where attention landed, not as the model 'reading carelessly'?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: The context window is a budget
topics.description: Everything the model can look at once has to fit inside a fixed window, measured in tokens. Attention does not hold evenly across it, and the middle fades first. So 'the model forgot my project' is almost always a budget spent badly, not a broken memory.
evidence: Explain why a rule you state once at the start can quietly stop working later in a long session
Explain why a bigger window is a ceiling to stay under, not a space to fill up
topics.critPrompt: In a long chat that lost the plot, can the student point to where the dropped rule fell in the window, and just say it again instead of blaming the tool?

grounding.ref: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, TACL 2024

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Embeddings, meaning as coordinates
topics.description: Every word, phrase, and image becomes a point in a huge space of many dimensions. In that space, closeness means similar meaning: courtyard sits near atrium and far from loading dock. This coordinate view is the base under search, generation, and multimodal reasoning.
evidence: Explain why two ideas a designer knows are related end up near each other, without anyone telling the model they belong together
Use the map-and-distance picture to describe what 'similar' means to the model
topics.critPrompt: Can the student explain why the model treats 'threshold' and 'entry' as neighbours, using coordinates rather than a dictionary?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: The joint text-image space
topics.description: Multimodal models train text and images into one shared coordinate space. So a photo of a courtyard and the words 'a photograph of a courtyard' land at almost the same address. That shared space is the whole reason 'make it like this reference' works at all.
evidence: Explain how a reference image and a text prompt can be compared inside the same space
Describe what it means that an image and its caption are trained to line up
topics.critPrompt: When a student uploads a reference, can they say what the model really does with it, which is find its coordinate, instead of 'it looks at my image'?

grounding.ref: Radford et al., Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP), 2021

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Dense and sparse territory
topics.description: The shared space is not filled in evenly. Styles that get photographed a lot form dense, well-mapped areas the model can steer through cleanly. Styles with little documentation sit in thin, sparse areas where the model fills the gaps and drifts. Naming this map is how we explain why some prompts obey and others quietly fail.
evidence: For two references, predict which one will steer cleanly and which will drift, and say why
Explain why a rare regional prompt gives confident but wrong results, and how that is just the model reporting thin coverage
topics.critPrompt: When a student's local-style prompt drifts, do they just write a longer prompt, or do they see they are in sparse territory and change the anchor image?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Seed, temperature, and re-runs
topics.description: A seed fixes the random starting point. Temperature sets how bold the model is when it samples. Together they explain why running the same prompt again gives a new picture, and how to make one you can repeat. Getting the same result twice is a control you hold, not luck.
evidence: Explain why fixing the seed lets you repeat a result, while re-rolling just gives you a different one without steering it
Describe what turning temperature up does to how spread-out the results get
topics.critPrompt: When a student wants the 'same image but change one thing', do they fix the seed first, or just press regenerate and hope?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Guidance, how hard it steers
topics.description: Guidance scale sets how strictly a diffusion model follows the prompt. Set it too low and the image wanders off the brief. Set it too high and it burns into stiff, over-bright results. The good work happens in the zone between. This is a different knob from the seed: it controls obedience, not the starting point.
evidence: Explain the trade-off between drifting off-brief and burning out, and where the usable middle sits
Say clearly what guidance controls and what the seed controls
topics.critPrompt: Shown an image that is either mush or scorched, can the student trace it to the guidance setting rather than the wording of the prompt?

grounding.ref: Cho et al., Diffusion Explainer, IEEE VIS 2024

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Conditioning and control inputs
topics.description: Generation does not have to run on text alone. You can also condition it on structural inputs: a depth map, an edge map, a reference image, a plan drawing. These force the output to hold geometry that a prompt alone would lose. Conditioning is how a grounded generator actually gets grounded.
evidence: Explain what a structural control input locks down and what it leaves free
Describe why a control image keeps the walls in place even when you change the prompt
topics.critPrompt: Is the student conditioning on an input that carries real design thinking, or just dressing up a weak drawing in a strong style?

grounding.ref: Zhang et al., Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models (ControlNet), 2023

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Text-to-image vs image-to-image
topics.description: Text-to-image starts the denoising loop from pure noise. Image-to-image starts from a noisy version of a picture you give it, so the more of the picture you keep un-noised, the more of its structure survives. Choosing between them is really choosing how much of the source image to keep.
evidence: Explain why image-to-image keeps the layout that text-to-image makes up fresh every time
Describe what you give up as you turn the denoising-strength setting up
topics.critPrompt: When a student wants to keep a building's massing but change the mood, can they say why image-to-image, not a fresh text prompt, is the right choice?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Upscaling and the resolution question
topics.description: Models make images at a working resolution, then add detail in upscaling passes. Those passes invent believable texture. They do not recover real information that was there. So a high-resolution image can look sharper while quietly making up grain, joints, and text you never asked for.
evidence: Explain why an upscaled render can gain lots of detail that means nothing
Tell apart real information and invented detail in a blown-up image
topics.critPrompt: Handed a crisp 4K render, can the student spot the upscaled detail that looks sure of itself but is made up?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: How video generation holds time
topics.description: Video models spread generation across many frames. They have to keep the world steady over time, so light, materials, and shapes stay put as the camera moves. Holding that steadiness, called temporal coherence, is the hard part, and it is where these systems most clearly break.
evidence: Explain why a generated clip can shift in material or lighting from one frame to the next
Name what temporal coherence asks a model to hold that a single still image never has to
topics.critPrompt: Watching a generated walkthrough, can the student point to the frame where the building stops being the same building?

grounding.ref: OpenAI, Video generation models as world simulators (Sora), 2024

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: 3D and world models
topics.description: A first look at systems that build 3D geometry you can move through, and at world models that hold a steady, explorable space instead of a flat picture. For a spatial designer, this is the frontier pointed straight at their own medium. It is also the least ready.
evidence: Explain the difference between a generated image, a generated 3D model, and a simulated world you can walk through
Name one thing a world model offers a spatial designer that image generation never can
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say why a steady, walkable generated space is a harder problem than a beautiful still, and why that matters to architecture in particular?

grounding.ref: OpenAI, Video generation models as world simulators (Sora), 2024

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Vector similarity search
topics.description: Because meaning lives at coordinates, finding 'the most similar item' turns into looking for the nearest points in that space. This is what lets a studio search its archive by intent, climate, or building type instead of by filename. It is the basic move that retrieval runs on.
evidence: Explain how 'find projects like this brief' becomes a distance measurement in that space
Describe what a vector database stores, and why plain folders cannot do the same job
topics.critPrompt: Can the student explain why searching by similar meaning is different from searching by keyword, using coordinates and distance?

grounding.ref: Pinecone, What is a Vector Database?, 2024

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Retrieval as context allocation
topics.description: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, pulls the few most relevant pieces from an archive and puts them near the front of the prompt, where attention still bites. So a small, well-chosen pull beats pasting in a million tokens. Our surprising claim is this: a studio's memory problem is really a retrieval problem, not a window-size problem.
evidence: Explain why pulling one exact piece can beat pasting in a giant block of context
Describe RAG as a smart way to spend the context budget, and tie it back to attention and the window
topics.critPrompt: When a student keeps pasting the same background into every session, can they name the retrieval step that should replace it?

grounding.ref: retrieval beats a bigger context window (RAG / Studio-Stack essay)

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Tool use, reaching the world
topics.description: On its own, a language model only predicts text. Tool use lets it call outside functions, like a climate API, a code library, or a drawing exporter, and then read the result back. Each tool gets described to the model, and the model decides when the job needs it.
evidence: Explain how a model that only predicts text ends up 'using' a calculator or an API
Describe what the model has to be told about a tool before it can call it
topics.critPrompt: Can the student explain why handing the model your existing studio software as tools is different from replacing that software, and why that difference protects human judgment?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Agents, goals, tools, memory
topics.description: An agent is a model put inside a loop. Give it a goal and it breaks the goal into steps, calls tools, keeps track of where it is, checks its own work, and picks the next move. A plain model answers a question, but an agent chases a goal. It is also less reliable, so checking its work is built in, not optional.
evidence: Explain the difference between asking a model a question and handing an agent a goal
Name the parts of the loop for one studio task: goal, tool call, memory, self-check
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say what changes about responsibility when the machine acts over several steps instead of answering once, and where the human has to catch it?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Fine-tune or retrieve
topics.description: There are two ways to make a model speak your studio's language. You can fine-tune it, so the knowledge lives inside the weights. Or you can retrieve, so the knowledge stays in an archive you can edit and feed in at the moment you ask. For most studios, the honest first move is retrieval, not training.
evidence: Take a real studio need and frame it as a fine-tune-or-retrieve choice, with the trade-offs on each side
Explain which kinds of knowledge belong in the weights and which belong in an archive you can retrieve from
topics.critPrompt: When a studio says it wants the model to 'know our work', does the student reach for training out of habit, or weigh retrieval first and say why?

grounding.ref: no-training / retrieval-first default (Training-Data and RAG essays)

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Open-weights or API
topics.description: Some models hand you their weights, so you can run and change them on your own machines. Others you can only reach through a provider's API. The choice trades control, cost, privacy, and the freedom to fine-tune against ease and top-end power. It is a structural decision, not a favourite brand.
evidence: List what open-weights access lets you do that an API does not, and the other way around
Match a studio's privacy and control needs to one path, and defend the pick
topics.critPrompt: When a studio worries about client-data privacy, can the student reason from how open-weights and API models actually work, instead of naming a favourite product?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Evaluating a model for a task
topics.description: You judge a model by the task in front of you: your briefs, your building types, and what a mistake would cost. You do not judge it by a leaderboard. Real evaluation means running the model on work like yours and reading where it holds up and where it breaks.
evidence: Build a small test set made from your own kind of work, and judge two models against it
Explain why winning a benchmark does not prove a model fits a studio's real work
topics.critPrompt: When a student picks a model, can they show evidence from their own task behind the choice, or only point to what is popular?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: One window, both modalities
topics.description: Once text and images share the same coordinates, image patches and words flow into one attention stream and get reasoned over together. It is not a language brain and an image brain with a translator in between. Multimodal reasoning is one set of attention weights running over a single mixed sequence.
evidence: Explain why a model can answer a question that needs both the picture and the words at the same time
Tell apart the shared embedding space and the single attention stream that reasons across it
topics.critPrompt: Can the student explain, without using a 'translator' picture, how a model reasons over an uploaded plan and a written question together?

grounding.ref: Liu et al., Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA), 2023

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The batch is a contact sheet
topics.description: Read a set of outputs the way a photographer reads a contact sheet. Look across the whole sheet at once, frame against frame, and mark the few worth enlarging. The skill is fast comparison, before any single image pulls you in.
evidence: Scan a set of 12 to 20 images. Mark the three frames worth enlarging, with a reason for each.
Point to something a frame shows only when set next to its neighbours, not alone.
topics.critPrompt: Watch how the student moves through the batch. Do they read across the whole sheet, or fall for the first strong frame?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Variation is not difference
topics.description: Two outputs can look different and still be the same idea in new clothes. That is variation. Difference is a real alternative that would send the project somewhere else. Re-rolling gives you more variation. Changing the brief is what gives you difference.
evidence: Sort a set into 'only varies' and 'truly differs'. Defend the line between them.
Show two outputs that look different but carry the same design decision. Then show two that look alike but differ in intent.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student which outputs are real alternatives, and which are the same image in new clothes.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Knowing when to stop
topics.description: Iteration needs a stopping rule, or it turns back into gambling. Stop when the brief no longer changes the output. Or stop when the output answers the question you actually asked. Going past that point buys images, not decisions.
evidence: Set the stopping point before an iteration run. Stop when you hit it.
For a finished set, explain why the last useful cycle was the last one.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student why they stopped where they did. Could they have stopped three cycles earlier?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Words for critiquing output
topics.description: To critique a generated image, you need words that carry a fix, not a mood. Not 'I like it' but 'the light comes from nowhere', 'the scale is unbelievable', 'this material lies', 'the caption flattens the design'. Precise critique is what makes the next cycle possible.
evidence: Critique one output using only points a peer could act on in the next cycle.
Take three taste-verdicts ('nice', 'off', 'boring') and replace each with a named fault that can be fixed.
topics.critPrompt: In crit, does the student name a fault the maker could fix, or only report a feeling?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Set the rubric before you generate
topics.description: Decide how you will judge the output before you make it. If you don't, the model's fluency will decide for you. A written rubric says what the image must do, must hold, and must avoid. It turns 'do I like it?' into a check you can defend.
evidence: Write a short rubric for the image you want before you generate. Then hold the outputs to it.
Show a case where the rubric you wrote first threw out a good-looking output your eye wanted to keep.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what criteria they set before generating. Did they hold to them when the pretty wrong answer showed up?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Same brief, different engines
topics.description: Run one brief through different families of engine, a dreaming one and a grounded one. Read what each one rewards and what each one distorts. The same words make different worlds. The comparison trains your ear for each machine's accent.
evidence: Run one controlled brief across two engine families. Name what each one kept and what each one lost.
Take a stray output and match it to the family that made it, from its usual strengths and failures.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student predict which family will serve a given phase, and show the comparison that taught them?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Defending AI work in jury
topics.description: Presenting AI-assisted work to a jury means saying what is still a guess and what is settled, what was generated and what was drawn. You defend the chain of judgment, not the image. The pin-up is not the proof. The decisions behind it are.
evidence: Present an AI-assisted scheme. Under questioning, say what each image is, and get it right.
Answer 'is this real?' with the decision chain, not a defence of the render.
topics.critPrompt: Under jury pressure, does the student defend the image, or the judgment that made it?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Build a personal failure catalogue
topics.description: Keep a running record of your own AI failures: the outputs that fooled you, the briefs that misfired, the good-looking images you fell for. This catalogue is the most honest map of your growing eye. It records what you did not yet know to distrust.
evidence: Keep a catalogue of your own AI failures. For each one, note the tell you missed.
Name one failure you repeat, straight from the catalogue, and how you now catch it.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what AI mistake they repeat most. The answer should come from a record, not a guess.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Generated, photographed, or rendered?
topics.description: Train your eye to tell a generated image from a photo and from a CGI render. Each one has its own tells in light, edges, repetition, and physics. Being fooled is data. Knowing why you were fooled is the training.
evidence: Sort a mixed set into generated, photographed, and rendered. Back each call with its tells.
Name the exact tell that gave away a convincing fake.
topics.critPrompt: Hand the student a mixed set. Can they name the tell, not just the guess?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Atmosphere is not information
topics.description: Some images carry mood. Some carry buildable information. Few carry both. A great-looking render can be full of atmosphere and empty of anything you could build. Mixing up the two is how mood gets mistaken for finished design. Ask what the image is for before you judge it.
evidence: Sort a set by whether each image carries mostly atmosphere or mostly information.
Take one atmospheric image. State exactly what buildable information it has and what it does not.
topics.critPrompt: When the student presents a beautiful image, ask what in it could be built. Watch whether atmosphere was standing in for information.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Draw over the output
topics.description: Sketching over a generated image on trace is judgment made physical. What you redraw is what you rejected. What you leave untouched is what you authored. The hand deciding what to fix is the designer taking the frame back from the machine.
evidence: Lay trace over a generated image. In drawing, mark every part you would redraw by hand.
Explain what drawing over the image showed you that just looking did not.
topics.critPrompt: Ask to see the trace over the render. The marks are the student's real reading of the image.

grounding.ref: Pen-based scribble/annotation refinement of generated images with professional designers (arXiv:2602.08830, 2026)

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Was the brief the failure?
topics.description: When a batch disappoints, the first suspect is your own brief, not the model. Before you blame the engine or re-roll, ask what the outputs show the brief really asked for. That is rarely what you meant. Critiquing your own brief is the mature user's first move.
evidence: Given a failed batch, find the fault in the brief before you touch the model.
Rewrite the brief to fix a failure you first blamed on the engine.
topics.critPrompt: When the student's outputs miss, do they reach for the re-roll, or for the brief?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Seduction is not quality
topics.description: The model is built to flatter your eye, and so is the performance of using it — displaying prompts, outputs, and stylistic speed is not the same as designing. The test is simple and hard: what decision does this work let me make? An image, or a display of fluency, that answers no design question is noise, however cinematic it looks.
evidence: Reject a beautiful output because it answers no design question. Name the question it fails to answer.
Tell apart an image that is good-looking and useful from one that is good-looking and empty.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what the prettiest image on their wall lets them decide. If the answer is 'nothing', the wall is decoration.

grounding.ref: The Lexicon of Algorithmic Virtue — the-lexicon-of-algorithmic-virtue

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: When not to generate at all
topics.description: The sharpest judgment is knowing when the machine should stay out. Sometimes a hand sketch, a site visit, or a conversation is the right tool and generation is the wrong one. Refusal is a design move. The confident 'no' is where taste shows most.
evidence: Name a stage of a real project where you kept the machine out on purpose. Defend that call.
Tell apart a task where generation adds value from one where it only adds noise.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student where in their project they refused to generate. Was that a reasoned call, or just habit?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Coherence across a set
topics.description: Judging a visual family means judging how the images relate, not each image alone. Is the light consistent? Is the scale believable from frame to frame? Is the same material actually the same material? Coherence is a call you make across the whole set, and it is where families quietly fall apart.
evidence: Check a 3 to 4 image family for consistent light, scale, and material across the set.
Find the one frame that breaks a family's coherence, and say what breaks it.
topics.critPrompt: For the student's visual family, ask whether the images belong to one project, or just share a folder.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Route the task, not the app
topics.description: Match each design task to the kind of engine it needs: reasoning, dreaming, grounded, data, geometry, or cinema. Make that choice before you open any app. The skill is picking the right kind of intelligence for the job, not memorising a list of tools.
evidence: Given six studio tasks, sort each into an engine family and defend the choice
Explain why the same task needs a different engine family at concept stage than at delivery
topics.critPrompt: When the student reaches for a tool, first ask what family the task belongs to. Do they choose by the goal, or by the brand they happen to know?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Drafts, minutes and specs, verified
topics.description: Use AI to draft the studio's writing: meeting minutes, specifications, letters, schedules. Then check every important claim against a primary source before it leaves the studio. Fast on the draft, strict on the facts.
evidence: Draft a set of minutes with AI, then mark each fact as verified or unverified before sending them out
Catch one spec figure the AI stated confidently and got wrong
topics.critPrompt: For a document the student drafted with AI, ask which lines they checked, and against what. The unchecked lines are the liability.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Budget cost and time
topics.description: Treat generation cost and turnaround time as real line items in your project timeline. A render batch, a video pass, an agent run: each one spends money and time. Budgeting them is the same discipline as pricing a detail before you draw five hundred of it.
evidence: Estimate the money and the time one design task's AI stage will cost, before running it
Reshuffle a tight timeline when the chosen engine turns out too slow or too costly for the deadline
topics.critPrompt: Ask what the project's AI stage cost in money and in hours. Did the schedule plan for it, or absorb it by surprise?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Files a stranger can navigate
topics.description: Name and organise your working files so a newcomer, whether a new colleague or an AI, can find their way without being told. The folder, the version stamp, the naming convention: these are signposts for whoever arrives next.
evidence: Tidy a messy project folder so a stranger can find the current deliverable in one pass
Write a naming convention that a colleague and an agent could both follow on their own
topics.critPrompt: Hand the project folder to someone who has never seen it. How long before they find the live file, and know that it is the live one?

grounding.ref: legibility is a trained practice, not a knack

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Hand over in a stated state
topics.description: When you hand an AI-assisted file to a consultant, say plainly what it is: a rough idea or a resolved design, generated or drawn, checked or unchecked. Either the handover carries its own status, or the consultant inherits a fiction.
evidence: Prepare a consultant handover pack and label the status of each file clearly
Explain the professional risk of sending a generated image to an engineer with no status attached
topics.critPrompt: In a mock handover, does the cover note keep each file's status honest? Or does a good-looking render travel as if it were a resolved drawing?

grounding.ref: the deliverable carries its own status

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: An honest, strong portfolio
topics.description: Show AI-assisted work in a portfolio that is both strong and honest. Make your judgment visible, keep the disclosure clean, and be ready to defend your authorship to a jury or an employer. Honesty is not a tax on the work. It is what makes the work yours.
evidence: Build a portfolio spread of an AI-assisted project that shows the brief, the iteration, and the judgment, not just the final image
Write the one-line authorship note that spread will carry
topics.critPrompt: On a portfolio page, ask what the student decided that AI could not. Does the page show that, or hide it?

grounding.ref: authorship follows judgment, shown not asserted

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Read the competition's AI rules
topics.description: More and more design competitions say what AI use they allow, forbid, or want disclosed. Read those rules and follow them before you enter, not after. That is a professional habit, not a formality.
evidence: Find and summarise the AI-use clause in a real competition brief
Draft the AI-disclosure statement an entry would need to meet it
topics.critPrompt: Before the student submits, ask where the competition's AI rule is, and whether the entry follows it. Can they point to the exact clause?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Teach juniors the judgment
topics.description: A senior's job is to pass on judgment, not tool tricks. You build support around a junior, then slowly remove it as they learn the standard. Knowing when to remove that support is the whole art, in the studio as in the classroom.
evidence: Coach a junior through one AI-assisted task, and name where you chose to step back
Tell apart teaching a tool from teaching the judgment that governs the tool
topics.critPrompt: Ask the senior student what they left the junior to decide alone. The stepping back, not the demonstration, is where the teaching happened.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Stage a studio's adoption
topics.description: A small studio takes on AI in stages, not overnight. Audit the workflow, pick a small set of tools, run a pilot on a real project, keep what worked, and review every quarter. Taking it in stages is what makes it stick instead of scatter.
evidence: Draft a staged adoption plan for a small studio, with a milestone for each stage
Name the pilot project and the quarterly review the plan needs to be real
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student where the plan says 'stop and review'. A plan with no point to pause and drop what failed is a shopping list, not a plan.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Verify loops in production
topics.description: Build verification into a running studio system, not onto it later. That means self-checking steps, limits the workflow cannot get around, and sign-off gates the work cannot skip. A guardrail the process can ignore was never a guardrail.
evidence: Design a verify step and a firm human sign-off gate for one automated studio task
Explain why a limit the workflow can slip past does not really constrain it
topics.critPrompt: In the student's system, ask what the work cannot do until a human says yes. If the answer is 'nothing', the guardrails are just decoration.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: The deliberate no
topics.description: Choosing, on purpose, not to use AI at a given step. You do it to protect the part of the work that is the point, or because another tool does the job better. A considered 'no' is a design decision, and it proves you actually mapped the workflow.
evidence: Name a step in a real project where AI was kept out on purpose, and defend the choice
Tell apart refusing AI on purpose from simply never thinking about it
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student where in this project they refused AI on purpose. A workflow with no 'no' has not really been examined.

grounding.ref: reduce friction, not judgment — know when to refuse
Willems, Khan, Huang, Camburn, Sockalingam & Poon, 2025 (arXiv:2510.19342)

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Write the motion brief
topics.description: Turning a still into motion has five steps. Lock the still. Write a motion brief that says what moves, how fast, how long, and what stays still. Explore variants. Pick one gesture. Lock the deliverable. The still is the score. The motion is the performance.
evidence: Write a full motion brief for one approved still before you open any video engine
Make a short clip, and show the note that explains why you chose its one motion gesture
topics.critPrompt: Ask what the clip shows that the still could not. If the only answer is 'it moves', the motion brief did no work.

grounding.ref: the still is the score, the motion is the performance

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Lock what must not move
topics.description: Every grounded generation, image or video, needs a clear statement of what must not change: the geometry, the type, the palette, a person's face, the aspect ratio. Naming what to keep is as much a design act as naming what to make.
evidence: Add a preservation block to one grounded prompt, then show the drift that appears when you remove it
List the parts of a scene that drift most often unless you lock them
topics.critPrompt: When a generation drifts, ask which preservation line was missing. The drift is usually a 'do not change' that nobody wrote down.

grounding.ref: state what must not change — the preservation block

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Discipline when time is short
topics.description: Deadline pressure is exactly when iteration falls apart into fifty-image gambling. Holding the discipline under time means changing one variable per cycle, curating fast, and keeping a log. That is what separates a studio that ships from one that gambles and hopes.
evidence: Run a timed iteration that changes one named variable per cycle and still lands the result
Explain why churning out volume and picking feels faster under deadline, but is usually slower
