topics.critPrompt: Under a mock deadline, watch whether the student tightens the brief or floods the engine. The panic move is the tell.

grounding.ref: iteration discipline matters most when time and cost are tight

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Your archive is infrastructure
topics.description: A studio's own drawings, specs, photos, and debriefs are not dead storage. They are the material a studio system searches through and, one day, trains on. Every finished project quietly becomes infrastructure for the next one.
evidence: Explain how a studio archive can be searched by design intent, not just by filename
Name what a debrief written today would teach a search system next year
topics.critPrompt: Ask what a studio's ten-year archive is worth to a machine. Is the studio filing it as an asset, or losing it as clutter?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Build the studio's brief library
topics.description: Collect the studio's brief patterns, prompt scaffolds, and templates into one shared library that new staff and machines both draw on. Version it like a contract. A scaffold everyone reuses is worth more than a clever prompt one person happens to remember.
evidence: Turn three one-off prompts into a versioned, reusable studio template
Explain why a shared brief library serves the new hire and the agent equally well
topics.critPrompt: Ask where the studio's good briefs live. In a shared, versioned library, or in one senior's head?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: One full thread, judgment throughout
topics.description: Carry one real project from brief to delivery, with every AI contribution passing through judgment you can state: routed, verified, curated, logged, disclosed. The senior proof is not a good image. It is a whole project you can account for.
evidence: Run one project end to end, and produce the log that shows where judgment governed each AI step
Present the project so a reviewer can trace every AI contribution back to a decision you made
topics.critPrompt: Follow one project from brief to delivery. Is there a single AI step the student cannot explain with a decision of their own?

grounding.ref: every machine contribution passes through stated judgment

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: What may be uploaded
topics.description: Decide what studio and client material can go into an outside model, and anonymise or hold back what cannot. Make that call before the upload, not after you regret it. Confidentiality and IP are the limits that convenience has to respect.
evidence: Sort a set of project materials into three piles: safe to upload, anonymise first, and never
Explain what a client contract or NDA means for feeding drawings to an outside model
topics.critPrompt: Before the student uploads a client's drawing, ask what in it should never leave the studio. Did they check before pasting?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Name the job, not the deliverable
topics.description: Intent names what the work is for, not the artefact you want back. 'Test whether one service spine frees the west wall' is intent. 'Render the lobby' is a deliverable. Only the first tells the model whether its answer actually helps.
evidence: Rewrite three deliverable requests ('render X') as statements of intent
Show a case where naming the intent changed which output counted as good
topics.critPrompt: When the student briefs a model, do they state the question the work should answer, or only the artefact they want back?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Criteria, or only plausibility
topics.description: With no stated criteria, the model returns what looks plausible. With criteria, it returns a judgement. Naming how you will judge the answer turns the model from a generator into a tester of its own output.
evidence: Add clear success criteria to a brief and show how the reply shifts from description to assessment
Judge two outputs against named criteria rather than by first impression
topics.critPrompt: Before generating, can the student state the criteria that will make the result usable or not?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The six-layer reasoning brief
topics.description: Intent, context, constraints, criteria, output form, iteration loop. This scaffold makes a brief to a reasoning model complete. It is the text-engine twin of the seven-slot visual brief. Skip a layer and the model fills it for you.
evidence: Write a complete six-layer brief for a real studio decision and label each layer
Take a weak LLM answer and name which layer you left unclear
topics.critPrompt: Given a flat model answer, can the student point to the missing layer rather than blaming the tool?

grounding.ref: AI Fundamentals for Architects (Starter Manual) — ai-fundamentals-for-architects-a

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: What a reference image says
topics.description: A reference image is a dense brief. But the model reads what the image looks like, not why you picked it. You have to name what in the reference you actually mean. If you don't, the model borrows the wrong thing.
evidence: Take one reference and list what a model would read from it versus why you picked it
Show two references that read as similar to a model but carry opposite design intent
topics.critPrompt: When the student pins a reference, can they say which quality in it the brief wants the model to carry, and which to ignore?

grounding.ref: Radford et al., Learning Transferable Visual Models (CLIP), 2021

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Style words and substance words
topics.description: 'Contemporary, warm, natural light' are style words. They return the average. 'Single-storey courtyard, board-marked concrete, north skylight, compressed entry' are substance words. They return your building. Most weak briefs are all style and no substance.
evidence: Split a real brief's words into style and substance columns and rebalance it toward substance
Rewrite a style-only prompt as a substance brief and compare the outputs
topics.critPrompt: Does the student's brief carry programme and geometry, or only mood words the model will average away?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The brief is a versioned record
topics.description: A brief is a document that changes over time, from v1 to v2 to v3. That history is the record of your design thinking. Keep the versions and your authorship stays visible. The reasoning can be traced long after the image is made.
evidence: Maintain a versioned brief across one project and annotate what each version changed and why
Rebuild the design argument for a finished piece from its brief history alone
topics.critPrompt: Can the student show the brief's version history and defend each change as a design decision rather than a reword?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Three prompt families, three registers
topics.description: You brief the same design intent three different ways: to a reasoning model, a dreaming engine, and a grounded generator. One brief discipline, three registers. Match the wrong register to the engine and you waste both.
evidence: Brief one project three ways (LLM, dreaming, grounded), so each reads as distinct
Name which register an engine needs before writing a word for it
topics.critPrompt: Can the student write three genuinely different briefs for one project, and justify each against its engine?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Briefing a dreaming engine
topics.description: You brief a dreaming engine in atmosphere and photographic language: light quality, time of day, lens, film register, a named sensibility. These words steer mood. They do not fix geometry. Asking them to fix geometry is the wrong job.
evidence: Write a dreaming brief that sets light, atmosphere and camera without locking down the plan
Explain why a photographic word changes mood but not what can be built
topics.critPrompt: Does the student's dreaming brief chase atmosphere on purpose, or leak precision the engine can't honour?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Briefing a grounded generator
topics.description: You brief a grounded generator in what to keep, what to label, and what format to return. This is the language of edits and presentation, not free invention. The brief protects the real input instead of dreaming past it.
evidence: Write a grounded brief naming what must not change, what to label, and the output format
Show a case where a 'preserve' instruction saved a real drawing from being overwritten
topics.critPrompt: Is the student grounding on an input worth protecting, and does the brief actually protect it?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Negotiating the model's defaults
topics.description: Every slot you leave blank, the model fills with its default. That default is the average, tilted the way its data is tilted. Briefing is talking those defaults down. You name what you mean before the default decides for you.
evidence: Predict the default a minimal prompt will impose, then write the brief that overrides it
Name a default the model kept applying until you named it and refused it
topics.critPrompt: Can the student name the defaults their brief quietly accepts, and choose which ones to fight?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Briefing in your own language
topics.description: Models lean heavily on English. Other scripts break into more tokens and land in thinner, less reliable parts of the model's world. You can brief in your own language. But you have to know what precision it costs, and when English carries the intent better.
evidence: Run the same brief in English and in another language, then compare how faithful each is and what it costs
Name one design idea from your own context the model handles poorly, and explain why the data makes it so
topics.critPrompt: Does the student choose the brief's language on purpose, knowing where their own tongue adds meaning and where it loses precision?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The brief-to-crit loop
topics.description: The studio loop closes through the brief: output, crit, revised brief, again. A crit that only judges the image stalls. A crit that rewrites the brief is what turns generation into iteration.
evidence: Turn one crit's findings into specific edits to the next brief version
Show a loop where the crit changed the brief, not just the image selected
topics.critPrompt: After critiquing an output, does the student go back to the brief, or to the re-roll button?

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Write so it can be found
topics.description: Name files, folders, and briefs so a machine and a colleague can find and reuse them later. Being easy to read is a property of the work, not the searcher. The next person to open your work may be a teammate, your future self, or an agent.
evidence: Rename a messy project's files and briefs so a newcomer can find their way alone
Explain why a well-named brief is reusable material and an unnamed one is lost work
topics.critPrompt: Six months on, could a teammate or an agent find and reuse the student's brief from its name and structure alone?

grounding.ref: Kevin Lynch, The Image of the City, 1960

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The space program as brief
topics.description: Rooms, areas, and adjacencies written as a structured list are the oldest form of the brief. This is architectural programming, in Peña's sense. Now it is also machine-readable. An adjacency is data a model can act on. A vague 'open plan' is not.
evidence: Write a small space program with rooms, areas and adjacencies a model could act on
Turn a paragraph of client wishes into a structured, machine-readable programme
topics.critPrompt: Does the student's programme give the model relationships and quantities to work with, or only atmosphere to guess at?

grounding.ref: Architectural Programming, Whole Building Design Guide, National Institute of Building Sciences

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Structuring the brief for attention
topics.description: The model holds a limited window, and it pays attention unevenly across it. It is strongest at the edges and weakest in the middle. Put your load-bearing constraints at the top or in the most recent turn. Long threads cost you precision, not just space.
evidence: Put a brief's load-bearing constraints where attention holds, and explain the choice
Take a constraint the model ignored mid-thread and re-anchor it so it holds
topics.critPrompt: When a constraint gets dropped deep in a long chat, does the student re-anchor it, or assume the model still remembers?

grounding.ref: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle, 2023

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: AI is already in your day
topics.description: You already use AI without opening a single tool — face unlock, spell-check, and the feed that picks which images you see next. Before a designer uses AI on purpose, notice the AI already choosing what reaches your eyes.
evidence: Names three places in a normal day where AI already chose or changed what they saw
Explains that a photo from a feed was picked by a system, not shown at random
topics.critPrompt: Can you point to one moment today when a machine decided what you looked at?

grounding.ref: mt_AzTrT5ySCx, mt_EedcpioR0v (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Machines learn from examples
topics.description: Nobody writes these systems rule by rule. You show a machine many examples, it finds the patterns, and then it guesses about things it has never seen.
evidence: Explains in their own words that the machine learned from examples, not from written rules
Predicts that a system shown only cats will struggle with a dog
topics.critPrompt: Where did this system get everything it knows how to do?

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Everything it knows is data
topics.description: To a computer, a picture, a word, and a sound are all just data that people gave it. A model’s whole world is that data, and nothing outside it exists for the machine.
evidence: States that pictures, words, and sounds are all just data to a computer
Explains that a model cannot use anything outside the data it was given
topics.critPrompt: What is a photo, to the machine?
topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Machines get things wrong
topics.description: A machine only knows what it was shown, so bad or missing examples lead to confident wrong answers. AI is not magic — it is maths on data, and it fails in ways you can learn to predict.
evidence: Gives one reason a machine can be confident and wrong at the same time
Links a wrong answer back to missing or poor examples
topics.critPrompt: Why might a machine give a wrong answer and still sound sure?
topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: People stand behind the machine
topics.description: A machine is fast and tireless, but a person brings judgment and care. Knowing what each is good at tells you which choices to keep for yourself.
evidence: Names one thing a person does better than the machine, and one thing the machine does better
Decides which part of a task they would keep for a human
topics.critPrompt: Which choice in this task should a person make, and why?

grounding.ref: mt_oajUvqAiBJ, mt_u6SYiVx7FX (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Biased examples, biased machine
topics.description: If the examples a machine learned from lean one way, the machine leans that way too. The bias comes from the data, and a person is responsible for the choices it shapes.
evidence: Traces a lopsided result back to lopsided examples
Names who is responsible when a biased system makes a decision
topics.critPrompt: If the results lean one way, where did that lean come from?

grounding.ref: mt__BbOjiY5A5, mt_cVp_nop-5L (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Not everything you see is real
topics.description: AI can make images, video, and text that look real but are invented. Check the source, look sideways at other sources, and notice what tugs at your feelings — that is how you tell made-up from real.
evidence: Checks the source before trusting an image or clip
Names one feeling a fake was built to trigger
topics.critPrompt: Before you share this, how would you check whether it is real?

grounding.ref: mt_tzMr83pS8v, mt_WtO50EZQkf (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: AI costs energy and water
topics.description: Training and running AI uses real energy and water in real data centres. The same tools can help predict weather or cut waste, so it is a trade-off, not a free lunch.
evidence: States that training and running AI uses energy and water
Weighs a real benefit of AI against its real cost
topics.critPrompt: What does it cost to run this tool, beyond the screen?
topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Your data has value
topics.description: AI systems collect data about you — your clicks, your cookies, what a speaker hears. Someone holds that data and uses it, so know what you hand over before you upload anything that isn’t only yours.
evidence: Names two kinds of data a system quietly collects about them
Decides whether something is theirs alone to upload
topics.critPrompt: What are you handing over when you upload this, and to whom?
topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Chance, and how to name it
topics.description: Some outcomes are certain, some impossible, and most sit somewhere between on a scale from 0 to 1. Roll the same die twice and you get different numbers, but over many tries a pattern settles.
evidence: Places an everyday event on a 0-to-1 scale of likelihood
Explains why the same setup can give different results each try
topics.critPrompt: How likely is this, on a scale from impossible to certain?

grounding.ref: mt_iFFKZd-Vgv, mt_t0g2SlP404, mt_-bMnJcPJy8, mt_vmQJAtAFuy (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Points, grids, and distance
topics.description: A pair of numbers pins an exact spot on a grid, and points close together on the grid are close in place. You can slide, flip, and turn a shape across the grid without changing what it is.
evidence: Reads and plots a point from a pair of numbers on a grid

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Can the model read a plan?
topics.description: Reading a floor plan means holding geometry, connections, and symbols all at once. Models today read the text on a drawing well, reason about space only so-so, and fail at symbols — counting doors, windows, rooms. 'It saw my plan' is not 'it understood my plan.'
evidence: Give a model a plan and test it on three things: reading labels, judging adjacencies, counting doors
Explain the gap between the model reading text on a drawing and understanding the drawing
topics.critPrompt: Can the student show one thing a model reads on a plan and one thing it cannot, from their own test?

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: The surrogate model
topics.description: A surrogate is a fast machine-learning model trained to imitate a slow physics simulation — daylight, energy, wind. It answers in seconds what simulation takes hours to, but only inside the range it was trained on, so its limits must travel with the number.
evidence: Explain what a surrogate imitates and why it is faster than the real simulation
Name the validity limit that must be stated whenever a surrogate's answer is used
topics.critPrompt: When a student quotes a fast AI performance figure, do they also state the range the surrogate was trained on?

grounding.ref: Risk-aware early-stage building heating/cooling surrogate workflow with explicit validity limits (PMID: 42362706, 2025)
ML daylight/visual-comfort prediction at early stage (arXiv:2109.06450, 2021)

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Brief spatially, verify spatially
topics.description: Models are weakest exactly where architecture is strongest: spatial relations, counts, adjacencies. So every spatial clause you brief needs a matching check on the output — the brief and the forensic read are two halves of one loop.
evidence: For a brief with three spatial clauses, write the three checks you will run on the output
Catch one spatial instruction the model dropped, using your own check
topics.critPrompt: For every spatial thing the student asks for, can they show the matching test they ran on what came back?

grounding.ref: Chatterjee et al., 2024 — Getting it Right / SPRIGHT (arXiv:2404.01197)

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The first image traps you
topics.description: Seeing AI images while you ideate can lock you in, not free you up. In a controlled study, people using an image generator produced fewer ideas, less variety, and less original ones than people working with none. The tool sold as fuel for divergence can be an anchor.
evidence: Ideate on a brief with and without AI images, and compare how many distinct directions you got
Name the moment a generated image narrowed your thinking instead of widening it
topics.critPrompt: Can the student point to where an early AI image anchored the whole scheme, and say what they would do differently?

grounding.ref: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou & Velloso, 2024 (CHI; arXiv:2403.11164)

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Individual lift, collective sameness
topics.description: GenAI can raise one person's output while flattening the variety across everyone. Writers helped by AI wrote better-rated but more similar work, and idea-generators using it converged on look-alike ideas — a whole studio on the same model drifts toward one scheme.
evidence: Compare a class's AI-assisted outputs and measure how similar they became
Explain how a tool can help you individually and homogenise the group at once
topics.critPrompt: Can the student show where the class converged on one model's taste, and say what it would take to break out?

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The machine fixates too
topics.description: Fixation is not only a human trap — generative models fixate too, returning to familiar solutions and narrowing what they offer. Re-rolling the same model is sampling one imagination, not many.
evidence: Re-roll one prompt many times and map how narrow the model's range really is
Explain why switching models or reframing beats re-rolling for real variety
topics.critPrompt: When a student wants more variety, do they re-roll the same model, or change the model or the brief?

grounding.ref: Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI (arXiv:2502.05870, 2025)
Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas (arXiv:2602.20408, 2026)

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Prompting is thinking about thinking
topics.description: Working with these systems is mentally expensive: you have to know what you actually want, judge outputs against it, and decide how far to trust them. The struggle to prompt well is usually the struggle to state your own intent.
evidence: Take one failed prompt and rewrite it by first stating, in plain words, what you actually wanted
Explain why a vague prompt is often a sign of a vague intent, not a weak tool
topics.critPrompt: When a prompt fails, does the student sharpen their intent, or just add more words?

grounding.ref: Tankelevitch, Kewenig, Simkute, Scott, Sarkar, Sellen & Rintel, 2024 (CHI; arXiv:2312.10893)

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Friction is a feature
topics.description: Deliberate speed bumps — a prompt that challenges the AI, a forced pause, a question before you accept — measurably bring critical thinking back to AI-assisted work. The studio crit is exactly this kind of device, and stripping all friction out strips the thinking out with it.
evidence: Add one deliberate friction step to an AI workflow and show what it caught
Name a place where removing friction quietly removed a judgment
topics.critPrompt: Can the student point to the friction in their process that forces a decision, instead of waving the work through?

grounding.ref: "It makes you think": Provocations Help Restore Critical Thinking to AI-Assisted Knowledge Work (arXiv:2501.17247, 2025)

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Styles known unevenly
topics.description: The model's grip on architectural history is jagged — confident on heavily photographed canonical styles, prone to making things up on lesser-known ones. What comes back is resemblance, not reasoning about why a style is the way it is.
evidence: Prompt a canonical style and an obscure one, and compare how accurate each result is
Show one case where the model got the look of a style but missed the logic behind it
topics.critPrompt: Can the student tell where the model's style knowledge is solid and where it is bluffing, and prove it?

grounding.ref: Ploennigs & Berger, 2023 — Generative AI and the History of Architecture (arXiv:2312.15106)

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Digital twin means too much
topics.description: 'Digital twin' has no settled meaning. A study of 15,000-plus papers found the parts people assume — live data, simulation, AI — are often not there yet in real building twins. Literacy here is asking which capabilities a claimed twin actually has, not admiring the label.
evidence: List the capabilities people assume a 'digital twin' has, and check them against one real example
Ask three questions that separate a real twin from a label on a static model
topics.critPrompt: When someone says 'digital twin', does the student ask which capabilities it actually has before believing it?

grounding.ref: Abdelrahman, Macatulad, Lei, Quintana, Miller & Biljecki, 2024–25 (arXiv:2409.19005)

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Deskilling is a design decision
topics.description: Whether AI wears down your skill or builds it depends on how you use it. Hand over the struggle that builds understanding and you become a 'fragile expert'; use it in a structured, reflective way and you keep growing. Your AI habits are quiet decisions about which of your own skills stay sharp.
evidence: Name one skill your AI use is building and one it is quietly letting fade
Redesign one workflow so the AI removes drudgery but keeps the struggle that teaches you
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say which of their own skills their AI habits are exercising, and which they are outsourcing away?

grounding.ref: Systematic review of GenAI's impact on higher-order cognitive skills (PMCID: PMC13334428, 2025)
